answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
From our research we’ve seen that consequential accounting methods, particularly in the form of locational marginal emissions, have significant benefits in terms of aligning demand response and procurement actions with real emission reductions in energy grids (see the emissions shifting section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025). Additionally, we’ve seen that economic based incentives and average emissions factor based incentives can lead to insignificant decreases, or even increases in system emissions for demand response programs (see Gorka et al. "Electricityemissions. jl: A framework for the comparison of carbon intensity signals." 2025, Knittel et al. “Flexible Data Centers and the Grid: Lower Costs, Higher Emissions?” 2025), leading us to believe that consequential accounting is an important tool for ensuring that electricity based emissions reductions projects are properly incentivized. While there is not currently widely available data regarding marginal emissions, our study was able to successfully calculate marginal emissions across large transmission grids at a significant (~1400 bus) nodal resolution and thus we believe it is feasible to generate such data at a wide scale if requested of system operators.

As a final note, we submit that consequential emissions accounting also provides a way to generate carbon accounts for power transmission infrastructure and given the significant blockages to green energy generation created by transmission interconnection queues, it may prove beneficial to extend consequential accounting frameworks to transmission infrastructure based projects as well.

answers.label: Appropriateness of the TWG subgroup formula
Why the formula is or is not appropriate
answers.text:
The formula provided here matches the typical formulas used for carbon accounting with marginal emission rates and thus will align with the findings in current literature surrounding marginal emission rates and exhibit the useful properties of carbon accounting including proper summation without double counting (see the carbon accounting section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025). In addition we think it may be useful for the group to consider that this formula may be extended to low carbon forms of generation by considering the derated equation:
MWh*(MER - generation emission rate)
and that it can extend to demand response programs through considering the shifted power consumption.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: The scope of our investigations did not include secondary emissions effects from activities such as construction and so we are unable to comment on this matter with authority. However, the approach outlined here where secondary effects should be considered if they are expected to be significant when compared to a project’s primary consequential emissions impact sounds like a very reasonable approach

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text: The true operational consequential impact of electricity projects is determined by their impact on the realized dispatch, something which can vary significantly over seasons and even across hourly dispatch periods (see the hourly and seasonal characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025). This leads us to believe that any project calculating consequential emissions should update their emissions impact after the realization of each dispatch period with the highest granularity temporal data available.

answers.label: Why selected tests should be included
answers.text: The scope of our investigations did not include evaluations of a project’s additionality and so we are unable to provide useful comments on this matter.

answers.label: Details on operating margin methodologies
answers.text: By their definition, locational marginal emissions (LMEs) describe how system emissions change with respect to marginal changes in power demand/production and thus we believe the operating margin consequential emissions are truly described by the locational marginal emissions (LMEs) derived from the economic dispatch problem. If data describing LMEs is not available with a good temporal or spatial granularity, we believe the other selected approaches - particularly the Heat-rate/LMP based estimation and fuel-on-margin approaches can serve to approximate this. An accounting scheme should use a hierarchy of data availability as proposed in the market based methods consultation, for example (1) LME - hourly, (2) fuel on margin - hourly, (3) heat-rate/LMP - hourly, (4) LME - daily, etc. Regarding the difference based approach we believe that this is a poor approximation of LMEs as the system emissions can have significant changes across dispatch periods not just from load changes but also from (VRE) resource availability which leads us to believe such an approach could poorly approximate LMEs in some scenarios. Furthermore, it seems that the difference based approach assigns a single marginal emission rate to the entire system. This is inaccurate as due to transmission constraints we’ve seen that marginal emission rates can vary significantly across system nodes/regions (see the regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025).

answers.label: Details on build margin methodologies
answers.text: CAPEX modeling which correctly reflects grid development conditions serves as the true description of how an energy project will change the build margin of the grid Recent capacity additions, policy scenarios, and predictive CAPEX modeling seem to approximate CAPEX modeling of the true development conditions reasonably well. However, the average emission rate can be significantly different than the new capacity being displaced. Take for example the average emissions factor in coal heavy US grids such as in the intermountain west (see the regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025) where new capacity being added is in the form of gas and renewables, while the average emissions factor is much higher due to the high legacy coal penetration. In general, as renewables and cleaner new generation technologies come down in price, the average emission rate will become a poor approximation of the new capacity additions which electricity projects displace.

answers.label: Assessing model applicability to project types
answers.text: While a company’s ability to perform accurate modeling is outside the scope of our research, we’ve seen characteristics of marginal emission rates tend to remain quite similar within regions (see the regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025) and so creating a set of planning studies which define build margin rates for common project types across regions seems to be a reasonable approach to removing the knowledge and investment burden from entities wishing to perform such accounting on their projects. We additionally note that methods used to calculate marginal emission rates and long run marginal emission rates are project size agnostic, allowing for general calculation approaches to be developed and used across development types.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text: Long run marginal emission rates have shown promise for combining both the operating margin and build margin impacts of energy projects (Bhandarkar, R et al. “Are EVs Cleaner Than We Think? Evaluating Consequential Greenhouse Gas Emissions from EV Charging” 2025) and may be of interest to investigate as well.

answers.label: Why that spatial granularity ceiling
answers.text: From our simulations we’ve found that nodal granularity is important and leads to higher levels of marginal emission accuracy, and is thus always preferable. However, regarding the minimum level of granularity, from our research we’ve seen that in WECC and ERCOT regions tend to be well connected within themselves and thus tend to share marginal emission rate characteristics, however, when considering interregional transmission we observe more transmission constraints and thus can see significant differences in LMEs between regions. It should be noted there does also exist some intraregional congestion in some cases, particularly regarding wind development areas in the cheyenne-denver corridor and thus nodal LMEs are certainly preferable to larger granularity, however zonal emission rates or even balancing area and regional rates would likely be an overall reasonable approximation if necessary (see the carbon regional characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025).

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: In areas with high penetration of VRE resources we see significant hour to hour variance in simulation. In particular, for areas with high amounts of solar development we see marginal emissions trends which are highly correlated to the hour of the day (see the hourly and seasonal characteristics section in Cote and Sun. “Locational Marginal Emissions for Carbon-Aware Data Center Operations in Large-Scale Power Grids” 2025). If data allows, finer grain sub hourly rates would only improve accuracy, however, we recognize that this level of data granularity may be hard to access.

answers.label: Weighting approaches not feasible to implement
Other approaches for assigning margin weights
answers.text: While we have only preliminary results regarding the build margin aspect of consequential accounting, it seems as though the marginal impact on the build margin is best measured through a capacity expansion analysis or a long run marginal emission analysis as we’ve described previously. These approaches should provide information on impacts to both the build and operating margin and thus the respective weights will not need to be guessed but will rather be inherent to the methodology.
